items.originalTitle: Democrats see an immigration opening despite Stephen Miller’s rise
items.author: Samuel Benson, Myah Ward and Eric Bazail-Eimil
items.title: Democrats see an immigration opening despite Stephen Miller’s rise
items.summary: In the days before the midterm election, Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) felt confident that a blue wave could open the door to immigration reform. Cuellar was so bullish that he reached out to acting Immigration and Customs Enforcement director David Venturella and the Customs and Border Protection commissioner Rodney Scott to feel out areas of “common ground,” he said in an interview. Now Cuellar is one of several moderate Democrats angling to strike a deal with the White House, especially on reining in ICE officers and creating legal pathways to citizenship for some immigrants. They’re undeterred by President Donald Trump’s elevation of immigration hardliner Stephen Miller to chief of staff. And they’re buoyed by Trump’s recent admission that his deportations policy was “too tough.” Several of these Democrats have already placed calls to Trump and DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin to express a willingness to work together. Cuellar said he reached back out to Venturella and Scott after the election to try to schedule meetings. “If the president, as the president of the United States, makes a decision — and not a chief of staff — we can get the job done,” Cuellar said in an interview. “I’m sure we’re going to find a lot of differences, but if we sit down, we can definitely resolve them.” It’ll be a tough road: Securing buy-in from the White House becomes undoubtedly more complicated with Miller, a champion of the administration’s aggressive deportation push. Republicans in Congress have largely been willing to defer to the president on the issue. And Democratic leaders have questioned Trump’s sincerity and said they have no interest in working with Miller. The possibility will become even more tenuous once Democrats begin investigating the Trump administration, including the president’s immigration enforcement agencies. CBP and ICE did not respond to requests for comment. Neither did Democratic leaders Sen. Chuck Schumer and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries. Democrats like Cuellar, Sen.-elects James Talarico of Texas and Annie Andrews of South Carolina are aware of all of those hurdles. But they’re betting the midterms have created an opening for serious talks: Latino voters across the country swung hard back toward Democrats this cycle, and more and more Republicans are recognizing that their immigration agenda hurt them politically. Talarico and Andrews have publicly expressed interest in working with the president on immigration, and both ran on platforms that emphasized creating paths to citizenship for undocumented immigrants. “I’m ready to work with President Trump to fix this broken immigration system,” Talarico said in a statement. Inside the White House, there’s a recognition that the president will proceed however he so chooses, regardless of who the chief of staff is. Trump is accessible to outside voices — journalists, business leaders and lawmakers regularly call him directly — and often poses policy questions to aides and allies as he decides which direction he will go. “Everybody’s like, ‘Well, it’s never going to happen with Stephen Miller.’ Look, Donald Trump’s the president. I don’t care if Stephen Miller’s the chief of staff or Susie Wiles or John Kelly or whoever the chief of staff might be,” said a person close to the White House, granted anonymity to speak about the internal dynamic. For Democrats, there’s a real political incentive to getting a deal done ahead of a critical 2028 presidential election — especially as the party seeks to win back voter trust on immigration and border security, policy areas that spelled doom for them in 2024. “You have these Democrats who flip red states, and it’s also to their self-interest, right? Not just to do rhetoric, and go big or go home, but actually come to the middle with the president, with the Republicans. Because if not, I think that the big lesson this election is, Hispanic voters are gonna flip back ... if they don’t see Democrats delivering anything the next two years,” said Rebecca Shi, the executive director of ABIC, a coalition of pro-immigration reform business executives. She added that there’s a lesson for Republicans, too, if they don’t come to the table: “They will lose the White House.” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis touted Trump’s immigration accomplishments, including border security, a drop in crime and the creation of the Homeland Security Task Force and said the president’s “strong immigration policy remains unchanged.” She said Democrats should work alongside Trump to “keep our southern border secure, remove dangerous illegal criminals from our communities, and stop the illicit trafficking of lethal drugs.” Democrats welcomed the president’s remarks on 60 Minutes on Sunday, when he said he was open to legal pathways for some unauthorized immigrants who haven’t committed crimes and are working and contributing to the economy. Mullin also floated an openness to a bipartisan immigration overhaul involving DACA, which could provide permanent legal status to some undocumented immigrants who arrived in the U.S. as children, even as he — and the president — have insisted that any proposal wouldn’t include amnesty. In a sign that Democrats have learned the lessons of the Biden administration , many of them are eager to pair reforms with border security measures. Cuellar, who will chair the Homeland Security Appropriations subcommittee in the next conference, has long suggested including guardrails on ICE in the next funding bill, such as requiring judicial warrants, rolling out body camera usage and restoring “sensitive locations” such as churches and schools as off-limits. Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.), another Democrat who has expressed interest in working with the Trump administration, said that beyond “talk,” it would help to see some smaller concrete policy shifts from the White House to affirm that Trump is, in fact, open to changes to the immigration system. “The way to do that is to have some reforms already at ICE — whether it’s shutting down these detention centers, giving certain level of protections, whether to veterans, so they don't get deported, to maybe parents of U.S. citizens, they don’t get deported — something to show that, you know, it's not just talk, this isn’t going to be a policy led by Stephen Miller,” he said. But Miller remains a bogeyman for Democrats, someone they view as responsible for the president’s most extreme immigration policies. As chief of staff, he can ensure he’s one of the last people in the president’s ear — and that the White House doesn’t bend to what he sees as unrealistic Democratic demands. “The reason why they wouldn’t do an amnesty deal, I believe, is because it would be the ultimate and most public contradiction of the central thesis of this entire political program as it was sold to voters,” said Mike Howell, president of the Oversight Project and a member of the Mass Deportation Coalition. “It would be the end of the America First coalition as it currently exists.” Democrats' distrust of Miller will also make it challenging for them to align on any potential deal with the White House. “Stephen Miller is the mastermind and architect of terror, and death, and illegality in this country, and he is not anyone who even understands truthfully what immigration policy should look like,” said Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-Calif). “No deals, man. No deals,” she added. The White House pointed to Miller’s experience on the Hill as a valuable asset. White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said unlike Democrats “who refused to work with the President and blocked many of his popular policies, Stephen Miller has a track record of spearheading bipartisan efforts: public safety reform, making our cities such as Washington, D.C. and Memphis safe again, drug pricing transparency, and unleashing a nuclear energy renaissance.” Lawmakers are waiting for the president to make the first move. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who will continue to lead his fellow Republicans when Democrats retake control of the Senate this January, told reporters after the election that “if there's something he wants to do there, we can have that conversation.” “There are always some landmines, which is why in the past the wheels have kind of come off, despite some really good efforts at trying to find a landing spot. But yeah we're open to something he wants to propose,” Thune added. Jordain Carney contributed to this report.

items.originalTitle: Scoop up three great 4K Blu-ray movies for $33
items.author: Cameron Faulkner
items.title: Scoop up three great 4K Blu-ray movies for $33
items.summary: A screenshot from the movie Sinners featuring Michael B. Jordan. | Image: Warner Bros. Gruv always keeps its proverbial fire hose of deals on movies running with a steady stream throughout the year, but the online seller operated by Universal Pictures is really letting it rip now ahead of Black Friday. The site has a page filled with 4K Blu-rays eligible for a “ three for $33 ” promotion, and the catalog covers a lot of genres and time periods. There are Hitchcock films, cult classics, animated gems, and more recent titles included that deserve a spot on your shelf. If I had to pick three of my own, here’s what I’d go with: Batman: Mask of the Phantasm , Rear Window , and Sinners . Or, maybe I’d swap one for First Man because I can never get enough of its tense opening scene, or BlackkKlansman because it’s just so good. There’s a lot to like with the promo catalog. However, if you don’t mind spending a little more, Gruv has plenty more titles at $12.99 each, including newer releases. Several big box office films are here, from Obsession and The Super Mario Galaxy Movie to One Battle After Another , Weapons , and the fairly recent 4K Blu-ray launch of the Wachowski sisters’ Speed Racer , to name a handful of examples. You have no excuses not to load up holiday stockings with some fantastic goodies for the cinephile in your life (even if that’s you).

items.originalTitle: Why Jensen Huang Should Not Be Reinstated as Nvidia's CEO
items.author: Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, Stephen Henriques and Steven Tian
items.title: Why Jensen Huang Should Not Be Reinstated as Nvidia's CEO
items.summary: Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang speaks during GTC Berlin on October 21, 2026. —Soeren Stache—Getty Images Nvidia's board has reportedly and wisely closed the door on Jensen Huang’s return, barely a week after boardroom pressure pushed him to resign as chief executive. A dubious outside campaign is still trying to pry it open. Tech leaders like SpaceX’s Elon Musk and Y Combinator’s Garry Tan have signed a petition demanding his reinstatement, while financier shareholders Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker have urged Nvidia's board via letter to “avoid a rush to replace Jensen.” That door should stay shut. Over 33 years, Huang built the company at the center of the AI era, but in our view, his conduct nevertheless made his position untenable. He misled directors about undisclosed relationships and oversaw a firm no one could check—a breakdown in trust that was magnified in China, where he advocated loosening export controls even as restricted chips reached Chinese military units and a Shanghai facility tied to Alice Huang’s network. The political push to restore him rests on the billions his most prominent advocates have riding on his customer-financing web and on misleading geopolitical spin, at the expense of genuine shareholder concerns and national defense. In the spirit of the transparency we ask of Huang’s advocates, we note that our upcoming book, When Machines Act: The Promise and Peril of Our Agentic AI Future , includes Huang’s own words, drawn from his commentary at our Yale Chief Executive Leadership Institute CEO forums. A breach of trust For 13 months , Huang maintained through spokespeople that his ties to Alice Huang, head of major customer Megaspeed, were strictly business. Only after the Financial Times reported Washington’s concerns about her did the Nvidia CEO confess the affair to general counsel Tim Teter. Even then, he assured Teter, who spoke with the board, that there had been no others. Four days later, the New York Times uncovered a second affair . The Megaspeed entanglement posed a textbook conflict of interest. Megaspeed bought billions of dollars of scarce processors and is under federal investigation , and Nvidia's own code of conduct flags personal relationships as a conflict risk. Nothing currently in the public record indicates Huang ever disclosed the affair or stepped aside from a single decision involving Megaspeed. Huang’s second relationship crossed a similarly bright governance line in that it involved an executive who reported directly to him. In the past, corporate boards at McDonald’s and Intel ousted chief executives over relationships with employees, and an ally working on Huang’s return conceded , “Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offense.” Those lapses unfolded inside an organization seemingly engineered to leave its leader unchecked, with roughly 60 direct reports , family in senior posts, and no clear successor , board chair, or chief compliance officer . When a board of directors can no longer trust a chief executive, removal is their duty. We would argue that Huang’s conduct would be unacceptable of any chief executive, founder or not. China’s record Nowhere did that breakdown in trust carry steeper stakes than in China, where Huang was Washington’s foremost advocate for looser export rules. Documents reviewed by Bloomberg place servers holding Nvidia's H800, H100, and H200 chips inside a Shanghai facility tied to Alice Huang’s network. Some of those units reportedly went first to Aperia Cloud Services, an official Nvidia Cloud Partner in Singapore, before being smuggled into China. The servers were pledged as collateral in January 2025, when all three chips were barred from sale to China, nearly a year before President Donald Trump’s December 2025 decision — lobbied for by Huang and backed by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick—to let Nvidia sell the H200 to approved Chinese buyers for a 25% U.S. government cut. Far more alarming, other top-tier Nvidia hardware reached a blacklisted institution with ties to China’s military , where American technology could be turned against the United States. Procurement records document A100 and H100 purchases by People’s Liberation Army units, and Reuters reports that a blacklisted defense university bought two H200s through a reseller in September. Neither source says Nvidia made the sales. Exporting controlled silicon to China’s military or blacklisted entities without a license is illegal regardless. China’s premier AI labs built their newest models on export-controlled hardware too. Their “innovation” rests partly on American chips they were banned from buying and American models they were barred from copying. A forensic study found the fingerprint of Nvidia's Blackwell chips in six Chinese frontier models, and Anthropic says it caught Chinese labs distilling its models at massive scale—raising the question of whether their “innovation” rests partly on American chips they were banned from buying and models they were barred from copying. The study neither pinpoints where the Blackwell hardware sat nor establishes whether its use violated any law. Even without smuggling, Chinese companies tap advanced chips in Southeast Asian data centers built expressly for them, a loophole that was legal until the Commerce Department’s recent rule . The Wall Street Journal reports that Nvidia told many overseas cloud partners to keep Chinese customers below a ceiling of 30% to 49%. A supplier policing that ratio knows the figure, and disclosing it would be an elementary first step toward accountability. In May 2025, three months after Dell cut off Aperia over diversion fears, Huang insisted there was “no evidence of any AI chip diversion.” Yet short seller Culper Research counts billings routed through Singapore swelling from 8.5% of Nvidia's revenue to roughly 20% over three years, hitting 22% in the quarter ended July 2025. The very next quarter, the standalone Singapore line vanished from company filings when Nvidia switched to reporting sales by customer headquarters. In financial statements, Nvidia has said that over 99% of controlled data-center revenue billed in Singapore came from US-based customers. But a buyer that books orders through a U.S. entity is not the same as an American end user. Megaspeed bought most of its hardware through Aivres, the California arm of Inspur, a Chinese server maker which has been blacklisted for supporting China’s military. Suggesting that Singapore’s surging billings reflected nothing beyond American demand strains credulity. Neither Huang nor Nvidia has been formally charged with a crime, and the company maintains it complies with the law. Where the board’s unfinished inquiry would ordinarily counsel patience, it seems clear to us that the push to restore him anyway points to the financial self-interest driving his backers. The money behind the campaign Under Huang, Nvidia remade itself into its customers’ chief financier, “a central banker for start-ups that needed chips and funding,” as The New York Times phrased it. Through July, its equity stakes ballooned from about $7 billion to $99 billion. It has agreed to conditionally guarantee up to $105 billion in leases for OpenAI’s Ohio campus, and one economist calculates it backstops up to $125 billion of a $500 billion financing program with Wall Street firms. Huang may have personally assembled this financial edifice, but the fractures were showing before the scandal broke. By August, Nvidia was negotiating billions in guarantees for buyers unable to afford its hardware outright. Colette Kress, Nvidia former finance chief and now interim CEO, halved Nvidia's initial commitment to OpenAI, and late that month the firm paused certain credit backstops for cloud operators. Without Huang, smaller “neocloud” operators could face a painful reckoning. Nvidia's backing was widely seen as a hedge against capture by its largest customers—hyperscalers such as Microsoft, Amazon, and Google, which together account for about half its revenue. Heavily indebted neoclouds such as CoreWeave, in which Nvidia holds a 7% stake , depend on a patron, and Huang was among their biggest champions. Now, Huang’s loudest defenders sit in that web. Public filings as of June 30 show Nvidia as the largest holding at Gerstner’s Altimeter, paired with roughly $600 million of CoreWeave. Baker’s Atreides owned both names too, alongside a dominant stake—roughly a third of its reported portfolio—in SpaceX. Nvidia, in turn, held a $21 billion stake in SpaceX in June, and Musk’s company is a major buyer of Nvidia's chips. Of course, financial exposure does not automatically make these investors wrong, but readers deserve to weigh their appeals to due process beside their stake in keeping the financing spigot open. “Many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen,” Musk warned over social media. Supply deals that hang on one man’s handshake leave an enterprise only as sound as his judgment. Let Nvidia's board do its job Then, there is the claim that Huang fell victim to a political hit. President Trump added to the confusion on Monday, telling reporters that “nobody’s proven that she’s a spy,” in reference to Alice Huang, and that national security “was not put at risk,” despite his own secretary of state, Marco Rubio, reportedly overseeing a memo warning that she was one. Regardless, Nvidia's directors acted on firmer ground—Huang’s assurances to the board clearly seem to have been false. No more persuasive is the rallying cry offered by Anduril founder Palmer Luckey: “China wants Jensen out, so I want him in.” In reality, China wanted Huang to stay in. True, Beijing’s security agencies curbed Nvidia purchases to favor Huawei, but whatever Beijing’s industrial planners may have wanted, China’s AI companies wanted Huang’s chips, and got them. Administration hawks, including Rubio and Scott Bessent, pressed to enforce the very restrictions Huang lobbied to loosen. Financial disclosures reviewed by the Washington Post suggest Trump held between $13 million and $62 million in Nvidia stock at the end of August, up from $615,000 to $1.3 million at the end of 2024, a period when his administration let the company sell advanced chips in China. The White House told The Pos t that independent managers handle his portfolio. Still, the people setting America’s chip policy and those profiting from it overlap uncomfortably. Huang’s defenders fall back on a related fatalism, arguing Washington had no choice except to keep selling advanced processors to China in exchange for rare earths. However, America depends less on China for these minerals than commonly imagined. What it lacks is sustained investment to extract and process them. One industry estimate puts a domestic mine-to-magnet supply chain at tens of billions of dollars, rising toward $100 billion over time. Against the $1.9 trillion erased from Nvidia's market value since its October peak, roughly 20 times that top figure, building domestic capacity looks cheap. A board that can be overruled by a petition has no function. Nvidia's directors deferred to Huang for years and intervened late, and reversing course under outside pressure now would merely extend a habit of deference. Instead, the board should let its investigation finish, restore standalone Singapore revenue disclosures, and select a successor on the merits. Huang spent 33 years building an enterprise the AI era cannot do without. Now comes the defining test of a great company—whether it can outlast the person who built it. Economists across the political spectrum, from Karl Marx to Joseph Schumpeter, have argued that the rapacious nature of capitalism leads to its own demise. History has proven them wrong so far.

items.originalTitle: The Fire TV Stick 4K Plus is on sale for less than Amazon’s entry-level streamer
items.author: Sheena Vasani
items.title: The Fire TV Stick 4K Plus is on sale for less than Amazon’s entry-level streamer
items.summary: Amazon no longer considers the midrange Fire TV Stick 4K Plus as part of its official lineup following the launch of it latest Fire TV Stick 4K, but that doesn’t mean the streaming device isn’t still good value. In fact, it’s an even more attractive option now that it’s dropped to $29.99 ($40 off) at Amazon and Best Buy in the run-up to Black Friday. That’s just $5 shy of its lowest price to date, rendering it cheaper than both the entry-level Fire TV Stick HD and its new midrange replacement, the Fire TV Stick 4K . Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Plus Where to Buy: $69.99 $29.99 at Amazon $69.99 $29.99 at Best Buy The Fire TV Stick 4K Plus still offers a good balance of price and performance. Unlike its replacement, it supports both Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, delivering more vibrant colors, better contrast, and immersive audio with compatible TVs and speakers. It does require a separate power adapter, though, whereas the newer model can draw power directly from your TV’s USB port. You also don’t get as much storage here as with the high-end Fire TV Stick 4K Max , though 8GB should be plenty for streaming apps like Netflix and Disney Plus. The Plus model also supports Amazon’s redesigned Fire TV interface, which my colleague John Higgins found to be an impressive update . It makes it easier to browse different content categories and pin your favorite apps for quick access. Thanks to Alexa Plus support, you can also press the voice button on the included Alexa Voice Remote to find something to watch, control compatible smart home devices like lights and thermostats, check sports scores, and more without getting off your couch. Just don’t expect a customizable shortcut button, as that’s exclusive to the latest Fire TV Remote. items.originalTitle: Reliving the drama: England and Argentina stars watch 1986 classic with fresh eyes
items.author: Marcela Mora y Araujo
items.title: Reliving the drama: England and Argentina stars watch 1986 classic with fresh eyes
items.summary: A new film about the historic World Cup quarter-final clash finds new angles for a new generation “Is there anything new to say about it?” Gary Lineker asked the producer Flora Fernandez-Marengo when she first approached him to take part in The Match, a documentary about the 1986 World Cup quarter-final between England and Argentina. Flora told an audience at the London film festival premiere of the film that she played her best card then and showed Lineker an image of Maradona with Queen in 1981, during the band’s tour of Argentina. Maradona wearing a union jack T-shirt and Freddie Mercury an Argentina strip. It worked. Lineker said yes. The rock’n’roll angle, with Brian May as a talking head, is one of the very few details the film-makers added to Andrés Burgo’s book, The Match, on which the documentary is based. The directors Juan Cabral and Santiago Franco play with the timeline, hopping between past and present across 91 minutes, the exact duration of the match itself. Anecdotes that now form part of Argentina’s football folklore are spliced with excellent archive material.

items.title: The world's soil is worth US$325 trillion: Why isn't it protected?
items.summary: The world has binding international agreements to protect the atmosphere, biodiversity and the high seas. But soil—an estimated US$325 trillion (A$473 trillion) natural asset that sustains life on Earth—has no dedicated international treaty.

items.summary: New Jersey university’s Republicans club invited Bovino, who oversaw Trump’s ICE surges, to speak on campus Hundreds protested outside a Rutgers University campus building on Monday night, jeering former border patrol commander Greg Bovino, who was inside addressing a crowd of about 25 people. The university’s Republicans club had invited Bovino to speak, calling him the “Great Commander” and the “GOAT” in social posts promoting the event at the New Brunswick, New Jersey, campus. items.originalTitle: Stellar pulsations reveal hidden 1.8-solar-mass companion
items.title: Stellar pulsations reveal hidden 1.8-solar-mass companion
items.summary: Massive stellar companions can be difficult to detect because they emit little visible light or show no obvious signs of accretion. Their gravitational pull, however, can be traced through the motion of nearby stars. In pulsating stars, regular brightness variations act as natural clocks, offering a way to find these hidden objects.
